label: prop1
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop1}
Let $d\geq3$, $s\geq 0$ and suppose $u:I\times\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{C}$ is a solution to $(i\partial_t+\Delta)u=F$. For any $t_0\in I$, 
\[
\||\nabla|^s u\|_{S^0(I)}\lesssim\||\nabla|^s u(t_0)\|_{L_x^2(\mathbb{R}^d)}+\||\nabla|^s F\|_{N^0(I)}.
\]
head: environment
name: Strichartz estimates

title: Proposition
body_md:
There exists a positive, radial function $Q \in H^1(\mathbb{R}^d)$  which solves the ground state equation \eqref{grounstate}. Moreover, $Q$ has the variational characterization
\[
J(Q) = \min_{u \in H^1(\mathbb{R}^d)\setminus\{0\}} J(u), \quad J(u) := \frac{\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)}^2 \|\nabla u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)}^2}{\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |u(x)|^2 (|x|^{-2}\ast |u|^2)(x) dx}.
\]
Moreover, $J(Q) = \frac{\|Q\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)}^2}{2}$, so that
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |u(x)|^2 (|x|^{-2} * |u|^2)(x) dx \leq \frac{2 \|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)}^2 \|\nabla u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)}^2}{\|Q\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)}^2}, \quad \forall u \in H^1(\mathbb{R}^d).
\]
head: environment
name: Existence of ground state

label: grondstate1
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{grondstate1}
The following two statements hold:
\begin{enumerate}

\item (Decay of the ground state) There exists a constant $\delta>0$ such that
    \[
   |Q(x)|+|\nabla Q(x)|\lesssim e^{-\delta|x|},
    \]
\item (Decay of the non-local term)  We have
\[
\big[|x|^{-2}\ast |Q|^2\big](x)\lesssim \frac{1}{1+|x|^2}.
\]
\end{enumerate}

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{grondstate2}
    For any  $p\in(1,\infty)$ and integer $k\geq0$, we have
    \[
    \||\nabla|^k Q\|_{L^p}\lesssim_{k,p}1 
    \]
head: environment
name: $W^{k,p}$ estimate of $Q$

label: firstq
title: Proof
body_md:
From Proposition \ref{grondstate1} we see that
\[
Q\in L^p\quad\text{for all }\quad p\in[1,\infty]\quad\text{ and}\quad |x|^{-2}\ast |Q|^2\in L^q\quad\text{for all}\quad q\in(\frac{d}{2},\infty].
\]
Recalling $Q$ satisfies the elliptic equation \eqref{grounstate}, therefore, by the Calderón-Zygmund estimate, we deduce that
\begin{equation}\label{firstq}
  Q\in W^{2,p}\quad\text{for all}\quad p\in (1,\infty).  
\end{equation}
                                                                                                
Noticing that for any $u,v\in W^{2k,p},\forall p>1$, we have
\[
\Delta^k \left[(|x|^{-2}\ast |u|^2)v\right]\in L^p\quad\text{for all}\quad p\in(1,\infty),
\]
by the Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequality and H\"older's inequality, then the desired estimate comes from Calderón-Zygmund estimate by iteration, starting with \eqref{firstq} and chain rule.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
We say that $u \in C_{t, \text { loc }}^0 L_x^2\left(I \times \mathbb{R}^d\right)$ is almost periodic  if there exists a spatial center function $x: I \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^d$, a frequency center function $\xi: I \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^d$, a frequency scale function $N: I \rightarrow(0, \infty)$, and a compactness modulus function $C:(0, \infty) \rightarrow[0, \infty)$, such that for every $\eta>0$, we have the spatial and frequency localization estimates
\[\int_{|x-x(t)| \geq C(\eta) / N(t)}|u(t, x)|^2 d x+\int_{|\xi-\xi(t)|\geq C(\eta) N(t)}|\hat{u}(t, \xi)|^2 d \xi \leq \eta, \quad \forall t \in I.\]

label: alcompact
title: Lemma

title: Proof
body_md: The argument to obtain this lemma follows along fairly standard lines (see e.g. \cite{TVZ2,Visan}), so we only outline a brief sketch here. The idea is to take an arbitrary sequence of times $t_n$ and apply the linear $L^2$ profile decomposition (see e.g. \cite{MV}) to $u(t_n)$. Using Theorem~\ref{MMRZthm} and stability theory, we can use the construction of a \emph{nonlinear} profile decomposition to argue that there must be exactly one profile in the profile decomposition (since in all other cases we obtain scattering for the solution $u$). This yields the desired compactness.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:weakYoung}
Let $1 \leq p < \infty$ and $1 < q, r < \infty$ satisfy
\[\frac{1}{q} + 1 = \frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{r}.\]
Then there exists a constant $C_{p,q,r} > 0$  such that for all $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^d)$  and $g \in L^{r,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^d)$  we have
\[\|f*g\|_{L^{q,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^d)} \leq C_{p,q,r}\|g\|_{L^{r,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^d)}\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^d)}.
\]

label: sequencelemma
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Our first step will be to argue for the existence of a solution that blows up in both time directions (and hence is almost periodic on the entire lifespan).

We let $\tau_n\to\sup I$ be an increasing sequence.  Applying Lemma~\ref{alcompact}, after passing to a subsequence, we may write 
\[
u(\tau_n)=e^{-ix\cdot\xi_n}\lambda_n^{-d/2}\phi\big(\tfrac{x-x_n}{\lambda_n}\big)+w_n=: g_n \phi + w_n
\]
for some group elements $g_n$ (corresponding to scales $\lambda_n$, Galilean parameters $\xi_n$ and translation parameters $x_n$) and functions $w_n$ satisfying $\|w_n\|_{L^2}\to 0$. 


We let $v$ be the solution to \eqref{1.1} with $v|_{t=0}=\phi$.  By the $L^2$ convergence, we have $M(v)=M(Q)$.  Moreover, as $u$ blows up forward in time,
\[
\|u\|_{L_{t,x}^{\frac{2(d+2)}{d}}((\inf I,\tau_n]\times\mathbb{R}^d)} \to \infty \quad\text{and}\quad \|u\|_{L_{t,x}^{\frac{2(d+2)}{d}}([\tau_n,\sup I)\times\mathbb{R}^d)} \to \infty.
\]
Therefore, by the standard stability argument, we know that $v$ blows up in both time directions, and  thus by Lemma~\ref{alcompact}, $v$ is almost periodic on the entire lifespan $\tilde{I}$.  

We now assert the following: there exist $\{s_m\}\subset\tilde{I}$ and group elements $\{g_m\}$ such that 
\begin{align}\label{th5v26}
\delta\big(v(s_m)\big)=\delta\big(g_mv(s_m)\big)\to 0\quad\text{as}\quad m\to \infty.
\end{align}
 Assuming \eqref{th5v26} for the moment, let us complete the proof of Proposition~\ref{sequ}:

First, passing to a subsequence, we may assume that
\begin{equation}\label{equ:dis2-m}
\delta\big(g_mv(s_m)\big)\leq 2^{-m }.
\end{equation}
Set
\[
\begin{aligned}
\tilde u_{m,n}(x)
={}&\lambda_n^{d/2}
e^{i(\lambda_nx+x_n)\cdot\xi_n-i\lambda_n^2s_m|\xi_n|^2}\\
&\times u(\tau_n+\lambda_n^2s_m,
             \lambda_nx+x_n-2\lambda_n^2s_m\xi_n).
\end{aligned}
\]
By construction,
\[
\lambda_n^{d/2}e^{i(\lambda_nx+x_n)\cdot\xi_n}u(\tau_n, \lambda_n x + x_n) \to \phi(x) \quad\text{in}\quad L^2.
\]
Thus, for fixed $m$ and all sufficiently large $n$, the standard stability argument gives
\begin{align}\nonumber
\|\tilde u_{m,n}(x) - v(s_m,x)\|_{L^2} &\leq C(s_m) \|\lambda_n^{d/2}e^{i(\lambda_nx+x_n)\cdot\xi_n} u(\tau_n,\lambda_n x + x_n)-\phi(x)\|_{L^2} \\\label{equ:difuvest}
& \leq C(s_m) o_n(1) \quad\text{as}\quad n\to\infty. 
\end{align}
Moreover, as $\tau_n\to\sup I$, we can also choose  sufficiently large $n(m)$ such that
\[
\tau_{n(m)}+\lambda_{n(m)}^2 s_m\to\sup I \quad\text{as}\quad m\to\infty.
\]
By \eqref{ppp}, \eqref{equ:dis2-m}, and \eqref{equ:difuvest},
\begin{align*}
\delta\bigl(u(\tau_n+\lambda_n^2s_m)\bigr)
&=\delta(\widetilde u_{m,n})\\
&=\inf_g\|g\widetilde u_{m,n}-Q\|_{L_x^2}\\
&\leq\inf_g\|gv(s_m)-Q\|_{L_x^2}
       +\|\widetilde u_{m,n}-v(s_m)\|_{L_x^2}\\
&\lesssim2^{-m}+C(s_m)o_n(1),
\end{align*}
where the infimum is over the symmetries in \eqref{ppp}.
Thus for each $m$, there exists $n=n(m)$ such that 
\[
\delta\big(u(\tau_{n(m)}+\lambda_{n(m)}^2s_m)\big)
\lesssim 2^{-m},
\]
so that Proposition~\ref{sequ} holds with $t_m:=\tau_{n(m)}+\lambda_{n(m)}^2 s_m$.

It therefore remains to prove \eqref{th5v26}.  

To this end, we will first argue for the existence of another almost periodic solution, which has bounded frequency scale.  The construction, which utilizes the notion of the normalization of an almost periodic solution, is standard by now (see e.g. \cite{TVZ2,Visan}).  Thus we will omit the details and instead refer the reader to \cite{TVZ2,Visan} for a clear and thorough exposition.

In particular, we may construct a solution $w:\tilde{\tilde{I}}\times\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{C}$, $[0,\infty)\subset \tilde{\tilde{I}}$ to \eqref{1.1} such that
\[
w(0) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \tilde g_n v(r_n)
\]
for some group elements $\tilde g_n$ and some sequence $\{r_n\}\subset\mathbb{R}$.  This solution satisfies $M(w)=M(Q)$ and is almost periodic on the entire lifespan, with some spatial center $x(t)$, Galilean boost $\xi(t)$ and frequency scale $N(t)$ satisfying $\sup_{t\geq0}N(t)\leq 1$.  
 
Arguing as we did above, we now observe that to prove \eqref{th5v26} it suffices to show that
\begin{equation}\label{th5v262}
\quad\text{there exists}\quad\{s_m^{\prime}\}\subset\mathbb{R}\quad\text{such that}\quad
\lim_{m\to\infty}\delta\big(w(s_m')\big)= 0
\end{equation}
In view of Lemma \ref{sequencelemma}, \eqref{th5v262} holds naturally and we can conclude the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $\delta\in(0,1)$, we can find $p_1\in(1,2)$ and $p_2>2$ such that
$$\frac{1}{p_1}=\delta+\frac{1-\delta}{p_2}.$$
Using \eqref{embeddingvp}, \eqref{interpo}, Lemma \ref{up-dual}, we obtain
\begin{align*}
\Big \|\int_{a}^te^{i(t-s)\Delta}F(s)\,ds\Big\|_{U_{\Delta}^2([a,b])}
\lesssim&\Big \|\int_{a}^te^{i(t-s)\Delta}F(s)\,ds\Big\|_{V_{\Delta}^{p_1}([a,b])}\\
\lesssim&\|F\|_{L_t^1L_x^2}^{\delta}\Big\|\int_a^t e^{i(t-\tau)\Delta} F(\tau) \, {d} \tau \Big\|^{1-\delta}_{V_{\Delta}^{p_2}}\\
\lesssim&\|F\|_{L_t^1L_x^2}^{\delta}\Big\|\int_a^t e^{i(t-\tau)\Delta} F(\tau) \, {d} \tau \Big\|^{1-\delta}_{U_{\Delta}^{p_2}}\\
\lesssim&\|F\|_{L_t^1L_x^2}^{\delta}\bigg\{\sup_{\| G \|_{V_\Delta^{p_2'} \left([a,b] \right)}=1} \Big|\int_a^b\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}F\bar{G}\;dx\;dt\Big|\bigg\}^{1-\delta}\\
\lesssim&\|F\|_{L_t^1L_x^2}^{\delta}\bigg\{\sup_{\|v\|_{U_{\Delta}^2([a,b])}\leq 1}\Big|\int_a^b\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}F\bar{v}\;dx\;dt\Big|\bigg\}^{1-\delta},
\end{align*}
and so \eqref{rrrt}   follows.

name: Upper bound for $E(P_{\leq k_0+4}u)$

label: f6.3
title: Proof
body_md:
Since $ \| \epsilon(t) \|_{L^2_{x}}$ is continuous as a function of $t$, so
the integral mean value theorem implies that  there exists $t_{0}\in [a, b]=J$ such that
\begin{equation*} 
\left\|{\epsilon}(t_{0}) \right\|_{L^2_{x}}^{2}
= \frac{1}{T} \int_{a}^{b}  \left\| {\epsilon}(t)  \right\|_{L^2_{x} }^{2} \lambda(t)^{-2}  \, {d} t.
\end{equation*}
Using the fact that $Q$ is real-valued, smooth, and has rapidly decaying derivatives and following the same argument as in the proof of Theorem \ref{t4.1}, we have for any $t\in J$
\begin{align}\notag
 E \left(P_{\leq k _0+ 4} u(t) \right)
  =& \frac{1}{2} \frac{|\xi(t)|^{2}}{\lambda(t)^{2}} \| Q \|_{L^2_{x}}^{2} + \frac{1}{2 \lambda(t)^{2}} \left\| {\epsilon}(t) \right\|_{L^2_{x} }^{2}
  - \frac{|\xi(t)|^{2}}{2 \lambda(t)^{2}} \left\| {\epsilon}(t)  \right\|_{L^2_{x} }^{2}
  \\\label{f6.3}
  &+ O \left(2^{2k_0}  \left\| {\epsilon}(t) \right\|_{L^2_{x}}^{2}  \right)
   + O \left(2^{2k_0} T^{-10} \right).
\end{align}
Thus \eqref{f6.1} holds at time $t_{0}$.

Since $E(P_{\leq k_0+4}u)$ is no longer conserved, we need to estimate the increment of this energy. By direct calculation,
\begin{align*} 
&\frac{d}{dt}E(P_{\leq k_0+4}u(t))\\
&\quad=\bigl(i\Delta P_{\leq k_0+4}u(t)+iP_{\leq k_0+4}F(u(t)),
\;P_{\leq k_0+4}F(u(t))-F(P_{\leq k_0+4}u(t))\bigr)_{L_x^2}.
\end{align*}
First, we  estimate
\begin{equation}\label{f6.5}
\int_{t_{0}}^{t'} \big( i \Delta P_{\leq k _0+ 4} u(t),
P_{\leq k_0+4}  {F} \big(u(t) \big)-F \big(P_{\leq k_0+4}u(t)\big) \big)_{L^2_x} \, {d} t.
\end{equation}
Since $P_{\leq k_0+4}F \left(P_{\leq k_0}u \right) - F \left(P_{\leq k_0}u\right)=0$, we have
\begin{align*}
&P_{\leq k_0+4}  {F}(u)-F \big(P_{\leq k_0+4}u\big)\\
=&P_{\leq k_0+4}\big(F(u)-F(P_{\leq k_0}u)\big)
+F\big(P_{\leq k_0}u\big)-F\big(P_{\leq k_0+4}u\big)\\
=&\sum_{(u_1,u_2,u_3)\in{\rm Sym}(A)}P_{\leq k_0+4}\big[(|x|^{-2}\ast(u_1\overline{u_2}))u_3\big]\\
&+\sum_{(u_1,u_2,u_3)\in{\rm Sym}(B)}P_{k_0+1\leq\cdot \leq k_0+4}\big[(|x|^{-2}\ast(u_1\overline{u_2}))u_3\big]\\
&+\sum_{(u_1,u_2,u_3)\in{\rm Sym}(C)}P_{\leq k_0+4}\big[|x|^{-2}\ast(u_1\overline{u_2})u_3\big]
\\
&+\sum_{(u_1,u_2,u_3)\in{\rm Sym}(D)}P_{\geq k_0+1}\big[|x|^{-2}\ast(u_1\overline{u_2})u_3\big]
,
\end{align*}
where ${\rm Sym}(\{a,b,c\})=\big\{(x,y,z):\;\{x,y,z\}=\{a,b,c\}\big\},$ and
\begin{align*}
    A=\{P_{\geq k_0}u,P_{\geq k_0-4}u,u\},\\ B=\{P_{\geq k_0}u,P_{\leq k_0-4}u,P_{\leq k_0-4}u\},\\
    C=\{P_{k_0\leq\cdot\leq k_0+4}u,P_{k_0-4\leq \cdot \leq k_0+4}u,P_{\leq k_0+4}u\},\\ D=\{P_{k_0\leq\cdot\leq k_0+4}u,P_{\leq k_0-4}u,P_{\leq k_0-4}u\}.
\end{align*}
Hence, we get
\begin{align*}
|\eqref{f6.5}|
\lesssim&\sum_{(u_1,u_2,u_3)\in{\rm Sym}(A)}\big\|\Delta P_{\leq k_0+4}u
\big[(|x|^{-2}\ast(u_1\overline{u_2}))u_3\big]\big\|_{L_{t,x}^1}\\
&+\sum_{(u_1,u_2,u_3)\in{\rm Sym}(B)}\big\|\Delta P_{k_0+1\leq\cdot \leq k_0+4}u \big[(|x|^{-2}\ast(u_1\overline{u_2}))u_3\big]\big\|_{L_{t,x}^1}\\
&+\sum_{(u_1,u_2,u_3)\in{\rm Sym}(C)}\big\|\Delta P_{\leq k_0+4}u\big[|x|^{-2}\ast(u_1\overline{u_2})u_3\big]\big\|_{L_{t,x}^1}
\\
&+\sum_{(u_1,u_2,u_3)\in{\rm Sym}(D)}\big\|\Delta P_{k_0+1\leq \cdot\leq k_0+4}u\big[|x|^{-2}\ast(u_1\overline{u_2})u_3\big]\big\|_{L_{t,x}^1}.
\end{align*}
Returning to the pairing in \eqref{f6.5}, expand using
$u=P_{\leq k_0}u+P_{\geq k_0}u$.
For a term with one high-frequency factor, write the commutator as
the outer projection error plus the term in which
$1-P_{\leq k_0+4}$ acts on that factor. Their output frequencies are
at least $16\cdot2^{k_0}$ and $12\cdot2^{k_0}$, respectively.
Both terms are therefore orthogonal to $P_{\leq k_0}u$ and
$F(P_{\leq k_0}u)$.
Here convolution with $|x|^{-2}$ preserves Fourier support.
Thus each nonzero pairing contains two high-frequency factors.
By H\"older's inequality, the Lorentz-space Hardy--Littlewood--Sobolev
inequality, Bernstein's inequality and Remark \ref{lorentzlongtime},
\begin{align}\label{bbv}
 |\eqref{f6.5}|
 &\lesssim 2^{2k_0}\|u\|_{L_t^\infty L_x^2([a,b]\times\mathbb{R}^d)}^2
 \|P_{\geq k_0}u\|_{L_t^2L_x^{\frac{2d}{d-2},2}([a,b]\times\mathbb{R}^d)}^2
 \notag\\
 &\lesssim \frac{2^{2k_0}}{T}\int_a^b
 \lambda(t)^{-2}\|\epsilon(t)\|_{L_x^2}^2\,dt
 +\frac{2^{2k_0}}{T^{10}}.
\end{align}

The term
\begin{equation*}
\int_{t_{0}}^{t'}  \left( i P_{\leq k _0+ 4} F(u(t)),
P_{\leq k_0+4}  {F} \left(u(t) \right)-F \left(P_{\leq k_0+4}u(t)\right) \right)_{L^2_x} \, {d} t
\end{equation*}
is estimated in the same way. The frequency support observation
above again supplies two high-frequency factors. Applying the
Lorentz-space Hardy--Littlewood--Sobolev inequality and Bernstein's
inequality, we obtain
\begin{align}
 &\left|\int_{t_0}^{t'}
 \big(iP_{\leq k_0+4}F(u(t)),
 P_{\leq k_0+4}F(u(t))-F(P_{\leq k_0+4}u(t))\big)_{L_x^2}\,dt\right|
 \notag\\
 &\qquad\lesssim 2^{2k_0}\|u\|_{L_t^\infty L_x^2([a,b]\times\mathbb{R}^d)}^4
 \|P_{\geq k_0}u\|_{U_\Delta^2([a,b])}^2
 \notag\\
 &\qquad\lesssim \frac{2^{2k_0}}{T}\int_a^b
 \lambda(t)^{-2}\|\epsilon(t)\|_{L_x^2}^2\,dt
 +\frac{2^{2k_0}}{T^{10}}.\label{bbv2}
\end{align}
Now \eqref{f6.3}, \eqref{bbv} and \eqref{bbv2} yield \eqref{f6.1} and we can conclude the proof of Theorem \ref{t4.2}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\eta_0,\eta_1$ be the constants in Theorem~\ref{t7.13}, and set
\[
\widetilde\lambda=\min_{t\in J}\lambda(t),\qquad
\alpha=\widetilde\lambda^{-2}a,\qquad
\beta=\widetilde\lambda^{-2}b,\qquad
\lambda_1(t)=\widetilde\lambda^{-1}
                 \lambda(\widetilde\lambda^2t).
\]
The rescaled function
\[
v_{\widetilde\lambda}(t,x)
  =\widetilde\lambda^{d/2}u(\widetilde\lambda^2t,
                            \widetilde\lambda x)
\]
is a solution of \eqref{1.1}. Apply a Galilean transformation and a
spatial translation to this solution, and continue to denote the
result by $v_{\widetilde\lambda}$. We choose these transformations so
that its modulation parameters satisfy
$\xi_1(\beta)=0$ and $x_1(\alpha)=0$. The modulation decomposition is
\[
e^{i\gamma_1(t)}e^{ix\cdot\xi_1(t)}\lambda_1(t)^{d/2}
v_{\widetilde\lambda}\bigl(t,\lambda_1(t)x+x_1(t)\bigr)
 =Q(x)+\widetilde\epsilon(t,x),\qquad t\in[\alpha,\beta],
\]
where $\widetilde\epsilon(t,x)=\epsilon(\widetilde\lambda^2t,x)$.
In particular,
\[
\|\widetilde\epsilon(t)\|_{L_x^2}
 =\|\epsilon(\widetilde\lambda^2t)\|_{L_x^2},
\]
and $\widetilde\epsilon$ satisfies \eqref{orthod}. By
\eqref{equ:assepsl2nor}, we have
	\begin{align*} 
	\int_{\tilde{\lambda}^{-2}a}^{\tilde{\lambda}^{-2}b}  \left\| \tilde{\epsilon}(t)  \right\|_{L^2_{x}}^{2}\lambda_1(t)^{-2}\, {d} t\leq\eta^2T\ll1,\\
1\leq\lambda_1(t)\leq T^{1/100},\quad \forall  \, t\in \left[\tilde{\lambda}^{-2}a,\tilde{\lambda}^{-2}b \right].
	\end{align*}
 Let $\tilde{s}(t):=\int_0^t \frac{\tilde{\lambda}^2}{\lambda \left(\tilde{\lambda}^2\tau \right)^2} \, {d} \tau, \
 \left[s_1',s_2' \right]:=\tilde{s} \left( \left[\tilde{\lambda}^{-2}a,\tilde{\lambda}^{-2}b \right] \right)=s([a,b])$. 
 By \eqref{f4.54} and \eqref{f4.55}, we have 
	\begin{equation*}
		\sup_{t \in  \left[\tilde{\lambda}^{-2}a,\tilde{\lambda}^{-2}b \right]}  \left|\frac{\xi_1(t)}{\lambda_1(t)} \right|
=\sup_{\tilde{s} \in \left[s_1', s_2' \right]}
\left|\frac{\xi_1 \left(\tilde{s} \right)}{\lambda_1 \left(\tilde{s} \right)} \right|
\lesssim  \eta^2T  \ll \eta_{0},
	\end{equation*}
    and 
	\begin{equation*}
		\sup_{t \in \left[\tilde{\lambda}^{-2}a,\tilde{\lambda}^{-2}b \right]}|x_1(t)|
= \sup_{\tilde{s} \in  \left[s_1', s_2' \right]} \left|x_1 \left(\tilde{s} \right) \right|
\lesssim  T^{\frac{1}{50}} \eta^2T^2 + T^{\frac{1}{100}} \eta T \ll T^{\frac{1}{25}}.
	\end{equation*}
Therefore, Theorem \ref{t7.13} can be applied  on $ \left[\tilde{\lambda}^{-2}a,\tilde{\lambda}^{-2}b \right]$, yielding 
	\begin{equation}\label{11.12}
		\int_{\tilde{\lambda}^{-2}a}^{\tilde{\lambda}^{-2}b}  \left\| \tilde{\epsilon}(t)  \right\|_{L^2_{x}}^{2}
        {\lambda_1(t)^{-2}  } \, {d} t
\lesssim \| \tilde{\epsilon} (\tilde{\lambda}^{-2}a )  \|_{L^2_{x} }
+  \| \tilde{\epsilon} (\tilde{\lambda}^{-2}b )  \|_{L^2_{x} }+  \eta^{4} T^{2+1/10}+ O \left({T^{-8}} \right).
	\end{equation}
Changing variables, \eqref{11.12} implies 
	\begin{equation*}
		\int_{s_1}^{s_2}  \left\| \epsilon(s)  \right\|_{L^2_{x}}^{2}  \, {d} s
\lesssim  \| \epsilon(s_1)  \|_{L^2_{x}} +  \|\epsilon(s_2) \|_{L^2_{x} } + \eta^{4} T^{2+1/10}
 + O \left( {T^{-8}} \right).
	\end{equation*}
Therefore, we conclude the proof of Theorem \ref{t7.14}.

label: finite:orbit-distance
title: Proof
body_md:
Without loss of generality, we assume $-1\in I$, $\sup(I) = 0$, and
		\begin{align*}
			\sup_{-1<t<0} \|\epsilon (t)\|_{L^2_x }\leq \eta_{\ast}.
		\end{align*}
		Applying the pseudo-conformal transformation, we obtain
\[
v(t,x)=|t|^{-d/2}
\overline{u\left(\frac1t,\frac{x}{t}\right)}
e^{i|x|^2/(4t)},\qquad t\leq-1.
\]
This is a solution of \eqref{1.1} which blows up backward in infinite
time. By \eqref{decomp}, with
$y=(x-tx(1/t))/(t\lambda(1/t))$, we have
\[
v(t,x)=\frac{e^{i\gamma(1/t)}e^{iy\cdot\xi(1/t)}e^{i|x|^2/(4t)}}
{(|t|\lambda(1/t))^{d/2}}
\left[Q(y)+\overline{\epsilon(1/t,y)}\right].
\]
Since
\[
\frac{|x|^2}{4t}
=\frac{|x-tx(1/t)|^2}{4t}
+\frac{x\cdot x(1/t)}2-\frac{t|x(1/t)|^2}4,
\]
removing the first term on the right from the phase of the $Q$ term
gives a function in the ground-state orbit. Thus, by \eqref{ppp}
and the radiality of $Q$,
\begin{align}\label{finite:orbit-distance}
\delta(v(t))
&\leq\|\epsilon(1/t)\|_{L_x^2}
+\left\|Q(y)\left(e^{it\lambda(1/t)^2|y|^2/4}-1\right)\right\|_{L_y^2}
\notag\\
&\leq\|\epsilon(1/t)\|_{L_x^2}
+\frac{|t|\lambda(1/t)^2}{4}\big\||y|^2Q\big\|_{L_y^2}.
\end{align}
Translate the origin of renormalized time to the physical time $-1$
and rescale so that $\lambda(s)\leq1$ for $s\geq0$.
Define $I(k)$ as in \eqref{f10.3}. By \eqref{f4.45} and
\eqref{f8.32}, there is a sequence $c_k\nearrow\infty$ such that
\[
|I(k)|\geq c_k,\qquad \lambda(s)\sim2^{-k}\quad(s\in I(k)),
\]
for all sufficiently large $k$.
For $s\in I(k)$, \eqref{f4.23} gives
\[
|t(s)|=\int_s^\infty\lambda(\sigma)^2\,d\sigma
\geq\int_{I(k+1)}\lambda(\sigma)^2\,d\sigma
\gtrsim c_{k+1}2^{-2k}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\frac{\lambda(t)^2}{|t|}\longrightarrow0\quad(t\nearrow0),
\qquad |t|\lambda(1/t)^2\longrightarrow0\quad(t\to-\infty).
\]
Together with \eqref{f8.32} and \eqref{finite:orbit-distance},
this implies $\delta(v(t))\to0$ as $t\to-\infty$.
For some sufficiently negative $t_0$, the solution $v$ therefore
satisfies the backward-in-time version of the hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{t2.3} on $(-\infty,t_0]$.
By time reversal and Theorem~\ref{t9.17}, $v$ is a solitary wave.
Hence $u$ is a pseudo-conformal transform of a solitary wave of the
form \eqref{pseudosoliton}.

name: Regularity of the eigenfunction

label: egen
title: Proof
body_md:
Clearly, $\chi$ satisfies the elliptic equation
    \begin{equation}\label{egen}
        -\Delta \chi+(1-\lambda)\chi=\phi_{Q^2} \chi+2Q\phi_{\chi Q}.
    \end{equation}
By Proposition~\ref{grondstate1}, $\phi_{Q^2}\in L^\infty$ and there
exists $\delta>0$ such that
\[
 |Q(x)|+|\nabla Q(x)|\lesssim e^{-\delta|x|}.
\]
We first bootstrap the integrability of $\chi$. Since $d\geq3$,
the restrictions of $K(x)=|x|^{-2}$ to $\{|x|\leq1\}$ and
$\{|x|>1\}$ belong to $L^1$ and $L^\infty$, respectively.
Using $Q\in L^q$ for every $1\leq q\leq\infty$, Young's and
H\"older's inequalities therefore give
\[
 \|\phi_{Q^2}f+2Q\phi_{Qf}\|_{L^p}
 \lesssim_p \|f\|_{L^p},\qquad 1<p<\infty.
\]
Starting with $\chi\in L^2$, global elliptic regularity applied to
\eqref{egen}, followed by Sobolev embedding, yields by iteration
$\chi\in W^{2,p}$ for every $2\leq p<\infty$.
Taking $p>d$, we obtain
$\chi\in C^{1,\mu}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ with $\mu=1-d/p\in(0,1)$.
In particular, $\chi$ is uniformly Lipschitz continuous.

Next we prove the exponential decay of $\chi$. To this end, we multiply both sides of \eqref{egen} by the function $\theta_{\epsilon}\bar{\chi}:=e^{\frac{\delta}{2}\frac{|x|}{1+\epsilon|x|}}\bar{\chi}$ and then integrate by parts, then we have
\begin{equation}\label{regu1}
\begin{aligned}
&\operatorname*{Re}\int\nabla\chi\cdot\nabla(\theta_\epsilon\bar\chi)\,dx
+(1-\lambda)\int\theta_\epsilon|\chi|^2\,dx\\
&\quad=\int\theta_\epsilon\phi_{Q^2}|\chi|^2\,dx
+2\operatorname*{Re}\int\theta_\epsilon\phi_{\chi Q}Q\bar\chi\,dx.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}


Noticing that $\nabla (\theta_{\epsilon} \bar{\chi}) = \bar{\chi} \nabla \theta_{\epsilon} + \theta_{\epsilon} \nabla \bar{\chi}$ and $|\nabla \theta_{\epsilon}|\leq\theta_{\epsilon}$ for all small $\delta,\epsilon>0$, using the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, it is easy to see that
\[
\operatorname*{Re} \big( \nabla \chi \cdot \nabla (\theta_{\epsilon} \bar{\chi}) \big) \geq \theta_{\epsilon} |\nabla \chi|^2 - \theta_{\epsilon} |\chi| |\nabla \chi| \geq \theta_{\epsilon} |\nabla \chi|^2 - \left[ \frac{1}{2} \theta_{\epsilon} |\chi|^2 + \frac{1}{2} \theta_{\epsilon} |\nabla \chi|^2 \right].
\]
Plugging it into \eqref{regu1}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{regu2}
  \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \theta_{\epsilon} |\chi|^2 \, dx \leq 2\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \theta_{\epsilon} \phi_{Q^2}|\chi|^{2} \, dx+4\operatorname*{Re}\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \theta_{\epsilon} \phi_{\chi Q}Q\bar{\chi} \, dx.  
\end{equation}
By Proposition \ref{grondstate1}, we know that $\phi_{Q^2}\lesssim \frac{1}{|x|^2}$ as $|x|\to\infty$. And hence there exists $R>0$ such that
\[
|\phi_{Q^2}(x)| \leq \frac{1}{4}, \quad |x| \geq R.
\]
Using this fact together with $|\theta_{\epsilon}(x)| \leq e^{\frac{\delta}{2}|x|}$ we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{regu3}
   2 \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \theta_{\epsilon} \phi_{Q^2}|\chi|^{2} \, dx \leq 2 \int_{|x| \leq R} e^{\frac{\delta}{2}|x|} \phi_{Q^2}|\chi|^{2} \, dx + \frac{1}{2} \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \theta_{\epsilon} |\chi|^2 \, dx. 
\end{equation}
Substituting this inequality into \eqref{regu2} gives
\begin{align*}
\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\theta_{\epsilon}|\chi|^2\,dx
&\leq 4\int_{|x|\leq R}
 e^{\frac{\delta}{2}|x|}\phi_{Q^2}|\chi|^2\,dx
 +8\left|\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}
 \theta_{\epsilon}\phi_{\chi Q}Q\bar{\chi}\,dx\right|\\
&\leq C(\delta)<\infty,
\end{align*}
where $C(\delta)$ is independent of $\epsilon$.
Indeed, the kernel decomposition above and
$\chi Q\in L^1\cap L^\infty$ imply
$\phi_{\chi Q}\in L^\infty$, and
\[
\left|\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}
\theta_{\epsilon}\phi_{\chi Q}Q\bar{\chi}\,dx\right|
\leq
\|\phi_{\chi Q}\|_{L^\infty}
\|e^{\frac{\delta}{2}|x|}Q\|_{L^2}
\|\chi\|_{L^2}.
\]
Letting $\epsilon\to0$, we get
\[\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{\frac{\delta}{2}|x|} |\chi|^2 \, dx < \infty.\]
The finiteness of $\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{\frac{\delta}{2}|x|} |\chi|^2 \, dx$ is sufficient for us to obtain the desired decay property. In fact,
as $\chi(x)$ is uniformly Lipschitz continuous on $\mathbb{R}^d$, there exists $L > 0$ such that
\[
|\chi(x) - \chi(y)| \leq L|x - y| \implies |\chi(x)| \leq |\chi(y)| + L|x - y|, \quad \forall y \in \mathbb{R}^d.
\]
Naturally we also have
\[
|\chi(x)|^2 \leq 2|\chi(y)|^2 + 2L^2|x - y|^2, \quad \forall y \in \mathbb{R}^d.
\]
Consequently,
\[
|\chi(x)|^2 \leq 4|\chi(y)|^2, \quad \forall y \in B_{0}(x) := \{y : |x - y| \leq \tfrac{1}{2L}|\chi(x)|\}.
\]
Integrating both sides over $y \in B_0(x)$ yields
\begin{equation}\label{equ:chixcondchiy}
    \omega_d \left( \frac{1}{2L}|\chi(x)| \right)^d |\chi(x)|^2 \leq 4 \int_{B_0(x)} |\chi(y)|^2 \, dy.
\end{equation}
Since $\chi\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ is uniformly continuous,
$\chi(x)\to0$ as $|x|\to\infty$. Thus there exists $R_0\gg1$
such that $|\chi(x)|\leq1$ whenever $|x|\geq R_0$.
For such $x$, we have
\[
|x - y| \leq \frac{1}{2L} |\chi(x)| \leq \frac{1}{2L} \implies |y| - |x| + \frac{1}{2L} \geq 0, \quad  y \in B_0(x),
\]
which implies
\[
e^{|x|} \lesssim e^{|y|} \implies e^{|y| - |x|} \gtrsim 1.
\]
This together with \eqref{equ:chixcondchiy} yields
\[
|\chi(x)|^{d+2} e^{\frac{\delta}{2}|x|} \lesssim \int_{B_0(x)} e^{\frac{\delta}{2}|y|} |\chi(y)|^2 \, dy \leq \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{\frac{\delta}{2}|y|} |\chi(y)|^2 \, dy < \infty, \quad |x| \geq R_0,
\]
which implies $|\chi|\lesssim e^{-\delta_0|x|}$ with $\delta_0=\frac{\delta}{2(d+2)}$. And so \eqref{equ:chidecay} follows.

It remains to prove $\chi\in W^{k,p}$ for any $k\geq0$ and $p>1$. To this end, we observe that as $|\chi|\lesssim e^{-\delta_0|x|}$, $\chi\in L^p$ for any $p>1$ and hence by the Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequality and H\"older's inequality, implies $\phi_{Q^2} \chi+2Q\phi_{\chi Q}\in L^p$ for any $p>1$, which again by the Calderón-Zygmund estimate implies that 
    $\chi\in W^{2,p}$. Now using chain rule and the fact that $Q\in W^{k_0,p}$ for all $k_0\geq0$ and $p>1$,  the desired estimate comes from Calderón-Zygmund estimate by iteration.

body_md:
\label{positive1}
    Suppose that $\epsilon=\epsilon_1+i\epsilon_2\in H^1$  satisfies  $\|\epsilon\|_{L^2}\ll1$, $\|Q+\epsilon\|_{L^2}=\|Q\|_{L^2}$ and
    \[
    \epsilon\perp_{L^2}\{\chi,i\chi,\partial_{x_1}Q,\cdots,\partial_{x_d}Q,i\partial_{x_1}Q,\cdots,i\partial_{x_d}Q\},
    \]
    then there exists $c_d>0$ such that
    \[
    (L_{+}\epsilon_1,\epsilon_1)+(L_-\epsilon_2,\epsilon_2)\geq c_d\|\epsilon\|^2_{H^1}.
    \]
